name: Carnivore-ish / animal-based diet

card.summary: Paul Saladino's meat, organs, fruit, honey and raw dairy approach: a looser carnivore diet with plenty of testimonials and little controlled research.
card.note: Raw dairy carries food-safety concerns, and no trial has tested the diet as a whole.

quick.overview:
The animal-based diet centres on ruminant meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and often raw dairy, with limited fruit and honey for carbohydrate. It excludes vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds. It was popularised in the early 2020s by psychiatrist Paul Saladino as a refinement of the strict carnivore diet.

Proponents report better digestion, energy and mental clarity. Mainstream nutrition experts call it restrictive, and no clinical trial has tested the full pattern. Looksmax.org users post both enthusiastic essays and reports of poor sleep, fatigue and persistent acne after a year on it.
quick.mechanism: Advocates say animal foods are nutrient-dense and avoid plant defence chemicals such as lectins and oxalates, while fruit and honey add carbohydrate for energy. Short-term feeding research shows that an all-animal diet changes gut bacteria within days.
quick.risks: Concerns raised include missing fibre and plant nutrients, high saturated fat, and the safety of raw dairy. Saladino himself reported low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone on strict carnivore before adding fruit and honey, according to Grokipedia.

lead: The animal-based diet emphasises nutrient-dense animal products such as meat, organ meats, fish, eggs and raw dairy, with limited low-toxicity fruits and honey, while excluding vegetables, grains, legumes, nuts and seeds.[1] Wikipedia describes it as a looser variant of the carnivore diet, adding fruit, honey and raw dairy, and credits Paul Saladino with popularising the red-meat-based version.[2]

Saladino, a psychiatrist, wrote The Carnivore Code in 2020, founded the organ-supplement company Heart & Soil that year, and later shifted from strict carnivore to an approach including fruit and honey, saying strict carnivore had left him with low energy, poor sleep and low testosterone, according to Grokipedia.[1] Proponents claim improved digestion, mental clarity and chronic disease management, whereas mainstream nutrition experts regard the diet as restrictive with potential long-term risks.[1]
On looksmax.org the diet is discussed both as an optimal human diet in long essays and as a disappointment by users reporting poor sleep, fatigue and acne after about a year.[3][4]
infobox: Ruminant meat, organs, fish, eggs, raw dairy, some fruit and honey

paras: Ruminant meats such as beef and lamb form the base, with organ meats (liver, heart) as staples, fish and seafood, eggs and dairy that advocates prefer raw or minimally processed, and limited fruit such as berries and avocado plus honey.[1] Strict versions keep fruit and honey minimal; inclusive versions add more of these carbohydrate sources, and people with dairy intolerance may use A2 milk.[1]
Vegetables are omitted because of oxalates and lectins, and grains, legumes, nuts and seeds because of phytates and fibre, according to proponents.[1]

Grokipedia traces animal-heavy eating to early hominins, the Inuit and Maasai, and Vilhjalmur Stefansson's supervised meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital in 1928.[1] The carnivore diet gained attention around 2018, and the animal-based variant emerged post-2020 as a version adding low-toxin plants, spread through podcasts, books and social media.[1][2]

Saladino hosts the Fundamental Health podcast, formerly the Paul Saladino MD podcast.[1] Wikipedia notes that traditionalist carnivore advocates, by contrast, focus on regeneratively raised livestock and eggs, and that the meat-influencer movement has been described as fringe.[2]

No clinical trial has tested the animal-based diet as a whole. Related research includes a 2014 Nature study in which short-term consumption of diets made entirely of animal or plant products altered the gut microbial community and gene expression within days, with the animal-based diet increasing bile-tolerant bacteria.[5]

Two crossover or parallel studies tested supplements alongside animal-based feeding: cranberry powder over five days in 11 healthy adults attenuated diet-induced microbiota changes,[6] and a probiotic yoghurt study examined changes in gut microbiota during an animal-based diet.[7]

Observational research on the opposite pattern found that, in the Rotterdam Study, greater adherence to a plant-based diet was associated with lower insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes risk.[8] Such findings concern diet patterns in general populations and do not test carnivore-style eating directly.

Wikipedia reports that nutrition scientists, dietitians and physicians regard carnivore diets as extreme fads, citing lack of fibre, micronutrient shortfalls, raised LDL cholesterol and links between high red-meat intake and colon cancer and gout.[2]
No studies found of the animal-based diet as a complete pattern. Related feeding studies are limited to short-term microbiome trials in small groups of healthy volunteers.[5][6][7]

A looksmax.org thread presents a long, AI-assisted essay arguing that evolutionary, isotopic and clinical evidence supports an animal-based whole-food diet and that mainstream dietary advice rests on low-quality evidence.[3] A separate thread titled as a failure report describes about a year of eating a pound of meat, organs and fruit under 100 grams of carbohydrate, with worse sleep, low energy, ongoing cystic acne and bloating; replies include an unrelated claim that meat acidifies the body.[4]

timeline.event: Vilhjalmur Stefansson completes a supervised meat-only year at Bellevue Hospital.[1]
Paul Saladino publishes The Carnivore Code and founds Heart & Soil.[1]
A Nature study reports that animal-based diets alter gut microbiota within days.[5]

lore.intro: Users on looksmax.org post both advocacy and failure reports about the animal-based diet.[3][4]

claims.claim: An animal-based diet is the optimal human diet.
claims.believers: An essay-length forum post argues that evolutionary, stable-isotope and clinical evidence supports animal foods and that mainstream guidance relies on weak epidemiology.[3] Saladino-style advocates add that nose-to-tail eating maximises vitamin and mineral intake.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that nutrition professionals regard carnivore-style diets as fads, and no clinical trial has tested the pattern.[2]

claims.claim: It clears acne and fixes sleep and energy.
claims.believers: Some users expect it to be a miracle cure; Grokipedia reports proponents claiming improved digestion and mental clarity.[1]
claims.experts: No published study has examined acne or sleep on an animal-based diet.

claims.claim: The diet failed for some users.
claims.believers: One user reports a year of poor sleep, low energy, acne and bloating despite eating meat, organs and fruit.[4]
claims.experts: Grokipedia notes that Saladino himself reported low energy, sleep disturbance and low testosterone on strict carnivore before adding fruit and honey.[1]

claims.claim: Eating only meat acidifies the body, while vegetables alkalise.
claims.believers: A reply in the failure thread argues this and recommends a book on germ theory alternatives.[4]
claims.experts: No study cited here examines body acidification from meat-based diets.
